records.content: Start Sport Switzerland International Football People MyTech Lifestyle Start Sport Switzerland International Football People MyTech Lifestyle Lifestyle"The chikungunya cases in Ticino are a wake-up call for Switzerland" Tiger mosquito "The chikungunya cases in Ticino are a wake-up call for Switzerland" The Ticino cantonal medical officer is calling for preventive measures against the Asian tiger mosquito, as this species also transmits dengue fever. (File photo) Keystone At the moment, the risk to the public posed by the chikungunya virus is low, says Ticino’s cantonal medical officer Giorgio Merlani in an interview with the Keystone-SDA news agency. However, Switzerland will need to be prepared for the future. Keystone-SDA 07.11.2026, 09:01 Keystone-SDA: Giorgio Merlani, when did the four people affected by chikungunya fever test positive? Giorgio Merlani: “In mid-October, the chikungunya virus was detected in the blood of the patients. One of the four people had already experienced symptoms consistent with the virus in August but did not get tested. When the doctor encountered two other positive cases of the chikungunya virus in October, he recalled this case and tested that person as well.” Why is that? Do they all have the same doctor? Merlani: “Two of the four people who fell ill are related. The other two live nearby.” How are the four patients doing now? Did they have to be hospitalized? Merlani: “Fortunately, all four are doing quite well. They only had to go to the hospital for tests. Two of them mainly had the typical rash, while the other two mainly suffered from body aches.” Do you expect more locally transmitted cases to occur in the coming weeks? Merlani: “No, I don’t expect that to happen right now. But you should never say ‘never.’ There are only a few mosquitoes around at the moment. In addition, in collaboration with the University of Applied Sciences and Arts of Southern Switzerland (SUPSI), we’ve sprayed a substance in the residential area where those affected live that kills adult tiger mosquitoes. Furthermore, not a single tiger mosquito in Ticino has tested positive for the chikungunya virus so far.” Is it possible to kill the mosquitoes in question using a substance sprayed locally? Merlani: “Yes, that’s very effective, because a tiger mosquito flies a maximum of about 100 meters in its entire lifetime. Thanks to this measure and the onset of winter, the risk of contracting the chikungunya virus is low at the moment. But the outlook for the future is different. We need to be prepared. The four cases in Ticino are a wake-up call for Switzerland.” In your opinion, what measures will be necessary in the future? Merlani: “In addition to the usual, individual preventive measures against the proliferation of tiger mosquitoes, municipalities must also fulfill their responsibilities. In Ticino, some are already collaborating with SUPSI to release sterile male tiger mosquitoes. In addition, under SUPSI’s leadership, efforts are being made to control tiger mosquito larvae. Numerous egg-laying traps distributed throughout the canton also map the density, activity periods, and spread patterns of the mosquitoes. All of this has proven to be effective. However, caution is also advised for travelers arriving from areas with many cases of the chikungunya virus.” What should be done about this? Merlani: “If vacationers test positive for the chikungunya virus, they must cover themselves so that tiger mosquitoes cannot bite them. This is because the mosquitoes transmit the virus to other people after about a week.” Is Ticino once again a “gateway” for a new virus? Merlani: “Not necessarily; tiger mosquitoes are also present in German-speaking and French-speaking Switzerland. The four cases in Ticino represent a very limited outbreak. But the virus will return, and we will see larger outbreaks. It’s important that we’re prepared for this throughout Switzerland.” The Ticino health authorities, in collaboration with SUPSI and the Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH), have launched a surveillance program for the West Nile virus. The goal is to reduce the risk of new cases of West Nile virus; SUPSI’s Institute of Microbiology serves as the national center of expertise. Should the federal government take further action? Merlani: “The federal government should, if possible, support preventive measures against the tiger mosquito. Cases of dengue fever could also occur in the future. I would be more concerned about this disease than about chikungunya fever. The first infection with dengue fever is usually mild, but a second infection can be quite dangerous.” Found an error?
